As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and its associated pictures. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). In an encounter, the identified teacher interrupts the recorded questioner asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?" (牛在甚麼處). The deviation from an ordinary count of cattle is documentary: "the Ten Oxen" (十牛) functions as the proper name of a Chan verse-and-picture series, circulated, recited, questioned, and criticized inside the record.

Senses.Explanation: The formula “if so, then” is a questioner’s recurrent inference in public exchanges, immediately tested or overturned by the recorded reply. A conversational connective: 'being so' followed by 'then,' hence 'if so, then.' It occurs 6,045 times in 344 files representing 338 independent works. Chan encounter records give it a conspicuous turn-taking role: a questioner repeats or draws an inference from a respondent's answer, and that respondent may confirm, reverse, test, or reject the inference. Recorded replies call the inference wild talk, reverse its premise, block it with an image, ask for the student's own part, or demand how the claimed conclusion is carried out. These outcomes are deployments of the same connective, not new senses. Its distinctive role is the recurrent public-interview hinge where a proposed understanding becomes answerable to the next line.

Senses.Note: 8 exact witnesses from 8 independent works delimit this sense.
